items.title: Finite distributions, entropy, divergence, and stochastic matrices
items.statement:
For a finite nonempty set identified with $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, a **probability vector** is $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^k$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; it is the outcome-weight vector of a finite probability space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). Its Shannon entropy in natural units is
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

These definitions use finite sets only; entropy is between $0$ and $\ln k$, as proved where needed below.

items.title: Symmetric and antisymmetric swap-test measurement
items.statement:
Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. On $H\otimes H$ define the **swap** $F$ by $F(u\otimes v)=v\otimes u$ and linear extension. Define the symmetric and antisymmetric effects
$$P_+=(I+F)/2,\qquad P_-=(I-F)/2.$$
The “equal” outcome corresponds to $P_+$ and “unequal” to $P_-$. When $H\ne\{0\}$, the following theorem proves well-definedness as a two-outcome projective measurement and calculates its pure-product law. For $H=\{0\}$ the operators are still defined, but no density input or measurement interpretation under the cited nonzero-space convention is asserted.

items.title: Finite communication problem and protocol model
items.statement:
A **finite communication problem** consists of nonempty finite input sets $X,Y$, disjoint sets $YES,NO\subseteq X\times Y$ with nonempty promise $P=YES\cup NO$, and a required output bit on promised pairs. This is the finite-relation generalization of a binary-string promise problem ([[def-promise-problem]]): choose fixed injective labels $c_X:X\to\{0,1\}^*$ and $c_Y:Y\to\{0,1\}^*$, and encode a pair by
$$e(x,y):=1^{|c_X(x)|}0\,c_X(x)c_Y(y).$$
The unary length prefix makes $e$ injective, so $e(YES)$ and $e(NO)$ are disjoint subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$. This encoding only formalizes the relation; it is not a transmitted message or part of communication cost unless a protocol explicitly sends it. A protocol specifies who receives each input, the message schedule and number of rounds, each message alphabet or finite-dimensional register ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]), the local maps that produce messages, the referee's finite POVM ([[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]]) and output rule, and any shared randomness or entanglement. A quantum message state is a density operator, meaning nonnegative with trace one ([[def-qc-density-operator]]). Its worst-case error is the supremum of the probability of a wrong output over promised input pairs; its communication cost is the maximum total number of transmitted bits or qubits on any promised input. Local computation, referee computation, and shared resources are separately declared and are not silently included in that communication count.

In a simultaneous-message protocol (SMP), Alice and Bob each send one message to a referee without seeing the other's message. For classical private-coin SMP with no shared resource, conditional on inputs $x,y$ the two messages are independent, so their joint law is a product of their individual message distributions. For quantum SMP with no shared entanglement or randomness, the received state is a product of the two locally prepared density operators. These factorization properties are part of the stated resource model.
proof_obligations: Specify worst-case promised-input error and separate communicated bits/qubits from local work and shared resources.

items.title: Equality communication problem
items.statement: For $n\ge1$, the **Equality promise problem** has $X=Y=\{0,1\}^n$, YES set $\{(x,x):x\in\{0,1\}^n\}$ and NO set $\{(x,y):x\ne y\}$. The required output is $1$ on YES and $0$ on NO. This is a total promise problem, and a bounded-error protocol must meet its error bound on every pair.
proof_obligations: Use the total promise and fixed output convention.

items.title: Code-based quantum fingerprint
items.statement:
For $n\ge1$ and $N\ge1$, let $E:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^N$ be a binary code map. Define its relative distance by
$$\delta(E):=\frac1N\min_{x\ne y}d_H(E(x),E(y)),$$
where $d_H(u,v):=|\{i<N:u_i\ne v_i\}|$ and the minimum is over distinct inputs. Thus duplicate codewords are allowed and give relative distance $0$, and $\delta(E)\in[0,1]$; the minimum is over a nonempty finite set because $n\ge1$. For every such map, with no positive-distance assumption, let $m=\lceil\log_2N\rceil$ and use the ordered computational basis of the $m$-qubit index register, padding unused indices by zero amplitude. The **fingerprint state** of $x$ is
$$|h_x\rangle:=\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}|i\rangle|E_i(x)\rangle,$$
where $E_i(x)$ is bit $i$ of $E(x)$, indexed from $0$ to $N-1$. It is a vector in the $(m+1)$-qubit index-and-data register. The following theorem proves it is normalized and computes its overlap. This is a state definition; it makes no uniformity or encoder-time claim.

items.title: Simultaneous-message equality by quantum fingerprints
items.statement:
**Inputs:** Integers $n\ge1$, $N\ge1$, and $r\ge1$; a fixed binary code map $E:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^N$ known to both senders and the referee; and inputs $x,y\in\{0,1\}^n$. The parties use no shared randomness or shared entanglement. State preparation and local computation are permitted and are not included in the communicated-qubit count.

**Output:** A bit $b\in\{0,1\}$, where $b=1$ means the referee declares $x=y$ and $b=0$ means the referee declares $x\ne y$.

Set $m=\lceil\log_2N\rceil$ and $L=m+1$. Alice prepares $r$ copies of the fingerprint state $|h_x\rangle$ and sends the $r$ registers, each with $L$ qubits, to the referee. Bob prepares and sends $r$ copies of $|h_y\rangle$ in the same way. The referee groups the received registers as pairs $(A_j,B_j)$ in increasing order $j=1,\ldots,r$. For each pair, the referee appends a fresh control qubit $|0\rangle$, applies the Hadamard gate $H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, then applies one Fredkin gate to each of the $L$ corresponding pairs of message wires, using this fresh control qubit as the gate's control. The referee applies $H$ again and measures the control in the computational basis. If any test returns $1$, stop the loop and output $b=0$. If all $r$ tests return $0$, output $b=1$. Thus each sender transmits exactly $rL$ qubits, and the referee uses at most $rL$ Fredkin gates and $2r$ Hadamard gates.
proof_obligations: Expand the H-controlled-swap-H state and count transmitted wires and Fredkin gates; pad the index by zero amplitudes when N is not a power of two.

items.title: Fingerprint swap-test error and communication cost
items.statement:
Let $n,N\ge1$ and let $E:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^N$ have relative distance $\delta(E)=\delta\in(0,1]$. Equal inputs yield antisymmetric probability $0$; unequal inputs yield $p\ge p_0=[1-(1-\delta)^2]/2=\delta-\delta^2/2>0$. For $0<\epsilon<1$, set
$$r=\left\lceil\frac{\ln(1/\epsilon)}{-\ln(1-p_0)}\right\rceil.$$
The bounded loop in [[alg-qa-35-swap-test-fingerprint]] halts after at most $r$ tests. On $r$ fresh pairs, declaring unequal iff any anti outcome occurs gives worst-case error at most $\epsilon$, with $r(\lceil\log_2N\rceil+1)$ qubits sent by each party. If $N\le Cn$ and $C,\delta$ are fixed, this is $O((1+\log n)(1+\log(1/\epsilon)))$ qubits per sender, conditional on a supplied code with those parameters.
proof_obligations: Keep δ>0 and ε∈(0,1); handle δ=1; distinguish a supplied efficient code from the nonuniform existence result.

items.title: Public-coin and private-coin SMP are different models
items.statement: For each n≥1, a shared uniformly random pair r₁,r₂∈𝔽₂ⁿ lets Alice send (r₁·x,r₂·x) and Bob send (r₁·y,r₂·y); the referee accepts equality iff both bits match. Equal inputs always match and unequal inputs collide with probability 1/4. The shared seed has 2n bits and is a separately declared public resource; independent private seeds do not give this guarantee.
proof_obligations: Compute the collision probability and show replacing shared seeds by independent seeds fails on a specific equal input.
